Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] EvilTokens phishing email delivered with workers.dev / lookalike device-code lures · [LLM] Phishing verdict bypass: malicious workers.dev mail landing in Inbox · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Entra device registration to DRS via Authentication Broker (EvilTokens PRT follow-on) · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint DNS/HTTP contact to EvilTokens ghost-phishing infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] EvilTokens device-code phishing: new-IP sign-in to Microsoft Authentication Broker · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
EvilTokens device-code phishing: new-IP sign-in to Microsoft Authentication Broker AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins to the Microsoft Authentication Broker first-party client (AppId 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) via the OAuth device-authorization grant from an IP the user has never used with that app. This is the core EvilTokens token-theft step where a victim enters an attacker-generated device code on the real Microsoft login page, so no password is stolen and MFA is satisfied. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated EvilTokens TTP: device-code grant to the Microsoft Authentication Broker AppId 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e (Sekoia/Huntress/Microsoft Storm-2372). Device-code flow to this broker is rare for office workers, and the new-IP anti-join keeps FP low. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/device-code-phishing-ai-mfa-bypass • https://detection.fyi/elastic/detection-rules/integrations/azure/initial_access_entra_id_device_code_auth_with_broker_client/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/06/ai-enabled-device-code-phishing-campaign-april-2026/
ATT&CKT1528 T1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin legitimately enrolling a device via Company Portal/Authenticator device-code flow
  • Developers using `az login --use-device-code` or Azure CLI device auth from a new network
  • Conference-room / kiosk device registration where the same user signs in from an unusual IP
  • Traveling employee first sign-in from a hotel/airport IP to the broker
  • Break-glass or MDM onboarding runbooks that use device code
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "AzureCLI" and ClientAppUsed != "Browser" and ResourceDisplayName != "Microsoft Intune Company Portal"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, UserAgent and Country; confirm with the user whether they entered a device code they received by email/chat. Check if the same IP hit other users' broker sign-ins (spray). 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), require re-auth, and block the source IP; review Entra 'registered devices' for a rogue enrollment. 3) Hunt: pivot on the IP/UserAgent across SigninLogs for other victims, check AuditLogs for 'Add device'/'Register device' and new inbox-forwarding rules created after the sign-in.
let broker = "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e";
let Baseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where ApplicationId == broker
    | summarize by AccountUpn, IPAddress;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"   // Microsoft Authentication Broker
| where ErrorCode == 0                                            // successful token issuance
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountUpn, IPAddress            // first time this user+IP hit the broker
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Application, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, Country, City, UserAgent
| order by Timestamp desc
let broker = "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e";
let Baseline = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where AppId == broker
    | summarize by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where AppId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"   // Microsoft Authentication Broker
| where ResultType == 0                                   // successful sign-in
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, Location, UserAgent, OriginalRequestId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Entra device registration to DRS via Authentication Broker (EvilTokens PRT follow-on) AIInstallation High
Hunts a successful sign-in to the Device Registration Service resource using the Microsoft Authentication Broker client, the EvilTokens post-token step where the attacker registers a rogue device to obtain a Primary Refresh Token that survives password reset. Distinct pivot from the initial broker sign-in: it keys on the DRS resource, not just the app. Rationale: Uses the corroborated EvilTokens/Storm-2372 escalation path: Auth-Broker token → Device Registration Service to mint a PRT (Elastic ships the same DRS rule). Resource==Device Registration Service under the broker client is near-zero in normal user activity, so tier=alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://detection.fyi/elastic/detection-rules/integrations/azure/initial_access_entra_id_suspicious_oauth_flow_via_auth_broker_to_drs/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/entra-id-oauth-phishing-detection • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/06/ai-enabled-device-code-phishing-campaign-april-2026/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Entra device join / Autopilot enrollment for a new corporate laptop
  • BYOD registration through Company Portal that transits DRS
  • Intune bulk enrollment runbooks
  • Admin testing device registration during onboarding
  • Windows Hello for Business provisioning on a fresh device
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "MICROSOFT_DEVICE_REGISTRATION" and ClientAppUsed != "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients" or IPAddress !in ("<known-enrollment-egress>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user or IT actually registered a new device at this time; inspect the device object's OS/displayName/registration IP in Entra. 2) Contain: disable/delete the rogue device object, revoke sign-in sessions, and reset the account; enforce Conditional Access requiring compliant devices. 3) Hunt: correlate to the preceding broker device-code sign-in (UC1), check for new PRT usage, mailbox forwarding rules, and OAuth app consents by the same principal.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"   // Microsoft Authentication Broker
| where ResourceDisplayName == "Device Registration Service"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, ResourceDisplayName
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AppId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"   // Microsoft Authentication Broker
| where ResourceDisplayName == "Device Registration Service"

Endpoint DNS/HTTP contact to EvilTokens ghost-phishing infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoints resolving or connecting to the EvilTokens phishing domains reported by ANY.RUN (Cloudflare workers.dev decoys and lookalike DocuSign/OneDrive/Adobe hosts). Because the phishing HTML is AES-GCM decrypted client-side, network telemetry may be the only host-side artifact of the lure being opened. Rationale: Direct IOC hunt on the 20 EvilTokens domains + MD5 fcd1b654a0b3e8f85ca7cfdafe494d4b from the article's ANY.RUN feed; the workers.dev/lookalike DocuSign/OneDrive hosts are the ghost-phishing decoy infra. Single-source (ANY.RUN TI) so scoped as hunting, not alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/cybercrime/eviltokens-phishing-doesnt-steal-password/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A domain in the list gets sinkholed/re-registered by a legitimate party after the campaign
  • Security tooling / sandbox detonation from a corporate range resolving the IOC domains for analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment services pre-resolving submitted URLs
  • A benign service reusing a generic *.workers.dev subdomain that collides with the list
  • DNS logging of blocked queries that never completed a connection
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user and the process that made the request (ContextImageFileName/InitiatingProcessFileName — expect a browser); confirm whether the user opened a link from email/chat. 2) Contain: block the domains/IPs at proxy and DNS, isolate the host if a device-code sign-in followed, and force the user's token revocation. 3) Hunt: pivot the source IP/user into SigninLogs for a broker device-code sign-in (UC1), sweep EmailUrlInfo for the same domains, and add the domains to the blocklist across all egress.

EvilTokens phishing email delivered with workers.dev / lookalike device-code lures AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound email whose links resolve to EvilTokens campaign domains (Cloudflare workers.dev decoys and DocuSign/OneDrive/Adobe lookalikes), the delivery vector for the ghost-phishing device-code lure. Surfaces recipients so the SOC can pre-emptively reset before a device-code sign-in occurs. Rationale: Joins EmailEvents→EmailUrlInfo on the 20 EvilTokens IOC domains to find the actual phishing emails and their recipients, enabling proactive containment before the device-code token step. Sentinel/Splunk left blank: this tenant's Sentinel schema has no EmailUrlInfo equivalent and Splunk CIM Email has no clean in-message URL field, so the detection lives on Defender XDR mail telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/device-code-phishing-ai-mfa-bypass
ATT&CKT1566.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign newsletter linking a *.workers.dev app that collides with the decoy list
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation emails reusing similar lookalike domains
  • Re-registered/sinkholed IOC domain now serving benign content
  • Internal IT test messages sent to seed EvilTokens IOCs into filters
  • A shared workers.dev subdomain used by a legitimate SaaS vendor
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryLocation != "Quarantine"
Response runbook
1) Triage: list all RecipientEmailAddress that received the IOC links and whether DeliveryLocation was Inbox vs Junk/Quarantine; check UrlClickEvents for actual clicks. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge the messages tenant-wide (Threat Explorer), block the sender and domains, and reset/revoke tokens for anyone who clicked. 3) Hunt: correlate clickers to UC1 broker device-code sign-ins and UC3 DNS hits; expand on the sender infrastructure (SenderMailFromDomain, SenderIPv4) for sibling waves.

Phishing verdict bypass: malicious workers.dev mail landing in Inbox AIDelivery Medium
Directly targets the article's thesis ('breaking traditional email security'): inbound messages that Defender scored as Phish/Malware yet were still delivered to the user's Inbox, and that carry a Cloudflare workers.dev or EvilTokens lookalike link. Because the phishing HTML is AES-GCM decrypted only in the browser, verdicts can flip post-delivery, so this catches the residual bypass. Rationale: Keys on the bypass signal the article calls out: ThreatTypes=Phish/Malware AND DeliveryLocation=Inbox with a workers.dev/lookalike link — distinct pivot from UC4 (which does not require a prior malicious verdict). FP rate medium because verdict-vs-delivery races and re-graded mail exist. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/cybercrime/eviltokens-phishing-doesnt-steal-password/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/device-code-phishing-ai-mfa-bypass
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ZAP/post-delivery re-grade already moved the message but EmailEvents still shows the original Inbox delivery
  • User-created allow rule or safe-sender entry forcing delivery of a flagged message
  • Phishing-simulation platform mail intentionally delivered despite a phish verdict
  • Legitimate workers.dev-hosted app flagged as phish by a noisy heuristic
  • Bulk/graymail mis-scored as Phish then delivered
Suppression filter
| where DetectionMethods !has "Simulation" and SenderMailFromDomain !in~ ("attacksimulator.microsoft.com", "knowbe4.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the message is still in the user's mailbox (not already ZAP-purged) and whether the user clicked (UrlClickEvents); review DetectionMethods to see why it was flagged. 2) Contain: purge tenant-wide, block sender+domain, and if clicked revoke tokens and force MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: tighten the Safe Links/allow-list rule that let it through, and correlate recipients to UC1/UC3 for downstream device-code sign-ins.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'

falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:
    category: process_creation

detection:

            - '\wscript.exe'

            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fcd1b654a0b3e8f85ca7cfdafe494d4b") or SHA1 in~ ("fcd1b654a0b3e8f85ca7cfdafe494d4b") or MD5 in~ ("fcd1b654a0b3e8f85ca7cfdafe494d4b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fcd1b654a0b3e8f85ca7cfdafe494d4b") or SHA1 in~ ("fcd1b654a0b3e8f85ca7cfdafe494d4b") or MD5 in~ ("fcd1b654a0b3e8f85ca7cfdafe494d4b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fcd1b654a0b3e8f85ca7cfdafe494d4b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] REF6045 ClickFix fake Windows Update: Edge kiosk to fakeupdate.net · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Installation. REF6045 ClickFix fake Windows Update: Edge kiosk to fakeupdate.net AIDelivery High
Hunts the SCMBANKER ClickFix distraction stage where a batch script launches Microsoft Edge in kiosk mode pointed at fakeupdate[.]net to render a fake Windows Update screen while the toolkit downloads in the background. Article-specific because the parent is a cmd/batch process and the child is msedge with both --kiosk and the fakeupdate.net URL. Rationale: Anchors on the exact article strings 'msedge --kiosk' + 'fakeupdate.net' — a decoy Windows Update screen no legitimate admin workflow produces; Elastic and GBHackers both confirm the kiosk-mode Edge distraction stage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/mexican-banking-fraud-scmbanker-ref6045 • https://gbhackers.com/ref6045-uses-scmbanker-powershell/ • https://cyberpress.org/clickfix-powers-mexican-fraud/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Kiosk/digital-signage deployments legitimately launching Edge with --kiosk to an internal URL (not fakeupdate.net)
  • IT running Edge kiosk mode for a locked-down browsing station
  • Security awareness training simulating a fake-update lure
  • Automated UI testing harness driving Edge in kiosk mode
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","mshta.exe","explorer.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent process is a cmd.exe/batch invocation (not explorer/user launch) and that the URL is literally fakeupdate.net; pull the full command line and initiating user. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the msedge and parent cmd tree, and block fakeupdate.net plus 68.211.161.46 at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for bitsadmin jobs against 68.211.161.46, C:\Users\Public\run.vbs, and an HKCU Run value named 'run' created within the last hour.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msedge.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--kiosk" and ProcessCommandLine has "fakeupdate.net"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--kiosk" and CommandLine has "fakeupdate.net"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SCMBANKER toolkit staging via bitsadmin from 68.211.161.46 AIInstallation High
Hunts the SCMBANKER download stage where bitsadmin is used to pull the PowerShell toolkit from the REF6045 open directory at http://68.211.161[.]46/files/. Article- and IOC-specific because it pins bitsadmin.exe to the exact staging IP confirmed by Elastic telemetry. Rationale: Elastic and GBHackers both confirm bitsadmin pulling PS1 modules from http://68.211.161[.]46/files/ — a hardcoded staging IP in a LOLBin transfer command line is extremely high fidelity with near-zero legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/mexican-banking-fraud-scmbanker-ref6045 • https://gbhackers.com/ref6045-uses-scmbanker-powershell/
ATT&CKT1197 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate bitsadmin transfers to internal patch/software repos (different IP, not 68.211.161.46)
  • SCCM/BITS background update jobs to Microsoft-owned ranges
  • Admin manually testing a BITS job
  • Backup or telemetry tooling that wraps bitsadmin
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the full bitsadmin command line and the file destination paths; confirm the remote host is 68.211.161.46 and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the actual connection to that IP. 2) Contain: isolate the host, cancel outstanding BITS jobs (bitsadmin /reset), block 68.211.161.46, and collect any files written under C:\Users\Public and %TEMP%. 3) Hunt: enumerate the downloaded PS1 modules (cliente.ps1, avs.ps1, jujuzkt.ps1, clip.ps1) and look for run.vbs plus the HKCU 'run' persistence value.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "bitsadmin.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "68.211.161.46"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\bitsadmin.exe"
| where CommandLine has "68.211.161.46"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SCMBANKER run.vbs launcher spawning named PowerShell modules AIInstallation High
Hunts the SCMBANKER master-launcher stage where C:\Users\Public\run.vbs (via wscript/cscript) starts the toolkit's PowerShell modules in parallel. Article-specific because it keys on the exact module filenames (cliente.ps1, avs.ps1, jujuzkt.ps1, clip.ps1, etc.) spawned by a VBScript parent. Rationale: The module filenames are unique SCMBANKER artifacts confirmed by Elastic's teardown (cliente.ps1=C2 beacon, jujuzkt.ps1=banking monitor, avs.ps1=Remote Utilities downloader); collectively they are a signature no benign software emits. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/mexican-banking-fraud-scmbanker-ref6045 • https://gbhackers.com/ref6045-uses-scmbanker-powershell/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A local admin script coincidentally named clip.ps1 or ini.ps1 (mitigate by requiring a wscript/cscript parent or multiple module matches)
  • Backup/monitoring frameworks with generically-named .ps1 helpers
  • Developer test scripts sharing a short name
  • RMM tooling running vendor-named PowerShell modules
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe","explorer.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the launching parent is wscript.exe/cscript.exe running C:\Users\Public\run.vbs and that two or more distinct SCMBANKER modules ran on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the powershell and wscript tree, and remove run.vbs plus the HKCU 'run' Run value. 3) Hunt: pivot on jujuzkt.ps1 window-title monitoring (screenshots/keylogging), clip.ps1/clip2.ps1 clipboard CLABE swaps, and avs.ps1 Remote Utilities install across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cliente.ps1","avs.ps1","jujuzkt.ps1","jujuzkt2.ps1","clip.ps1","clip2.ps1","correr.ps1","ini.ps1","rotor2.ps1","mensaje1.ps1","remo.ps1","edifhjwe.ps1")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("cliente.ps1","avs.ps1","jujuzkt.ps1","jujuzkt2.ps1","clip.ps1","clip2.ps1","correr.ps1","ini.ps1","rotor2.ps1","mensaje1.ps1","remo.ps1","edifhjwe.ps1")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SCMBANKER persistence: HKCU Run value 'run' launching run.vbs AIInstallation High
Hunts the SCMBANKER persistence stage where an HKCU CurrentVersion\Run value named 'run' executes hidden PowerShell that launches C:\Users\Public\run.vbs at logon. Article-specific because it pins the Run-key value name and the run.vbs target confirmed by Elastic. Rationale: Elastic confirms 'Run key: HKCU\...\Run, value "run", runs hidden PowerShell launching run.vbs' — pinning both the value name and the C:\Users\Public\run.vbs target makes this a very tight persistence signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/mexican-banking-fraud-scmbanker-ref6045 • https://gbhackers.com/ref6045-uses-scmbanker-powershell/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate app registering a Run value that happens to reference a benign run.vbs in Program Files (not C:\Users\Public)
  • Login-automation scripts an admin deploys via GPO
  • Software installers writing a hidden-PowerShell Run entry for updates
  • RMM agent autostart entries
Suppression filter
| where RegistryValueData has @"\Users\Public\" or RegistryValueData has "-w hidden" or RegistryValueData has "-WindowStyle Hidden"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Run value data references C:\Users\Public\run.vbs and/or a hidden -WindowStyle Hidden PowerShell launcher; identify the writing process. 2) Contain: delete the Run value, quarantine run.vbs, isolate the host, and check the Startup folder for the same launcher. 3) Hunt: correlate to the bitsadmin staging from 68.211.161.46 and the module executions (cliente.ps1, jujuzkt.ps1); sweep the fleet for the identical Run value name 'run'.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "run.vbs" or (RegistryValueName =~ "run" and RegistryValueData has "powershell")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "run.vbs" or (RegistryValue =~ "run" and RegistryValueData has "powershell")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SCMBANKER forced reboot via 'shutdown /r /t 02' from script parent AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the SCMBANKER stage where, after establishing persistence, the batch/VBScript forces a reboot with 'shutdown /r /t 02' so the Run key re-triggers run.vbs. Article-specific because it pins the exact zero-padded '/t 02' argument and a script-interpreter parent. Rationale: The zero-padded '/t 02' delay argument is an unusual, generation-artifact-style string (a human types '/t 2'); combined with a script parent and the surrounding persistence it flags the SCMBANKER reboot-to-trigger step described by Elastic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/mexican-banking-fraud-scmbanker-ref6045 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/scmbanker-malware-uses-clickfix-lures.html
ATT&CKT1529 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/GPO maintenance scripts issuing a scripted reboot with a short timer
  • Software installers that force a reboot to complete
  • RMM patch-and-reboot automation
  • Kiosk provisioning scripts that reboot after setup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cmd.exe" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","tiworker.exe","trustedinstaller.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent is a script interpreter (not a service/installer) and check whether an HKCU 'run' Run value or run.vbs was created on the host in the minutes before the reboot. 2) Contain: if corroborated, isolate the host before/after reboot and remove the persistence value so run.vbs does not re-launch. 3) Hunt: pivot to the ClickFix Edge kiosk event, bitsadmin staging from 68.211.161.46, and post-reboot cliente.ps1 C2 beaconing on the same device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "shutdown.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/r" and ProcessCommandLine has "/t 02"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\shutdown.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/r" and CommandLine has "/t 02"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

REF6045 C2 / phishing-redirect infrastructure connections AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts host connections to the SCMBANKER C2, phishing-redirect, and Telegram-exfil infrastructure — the phishing landing bancaporinternetbbmx[.]online plus REF6045 domains and staging IPs. Article/IOC-specific: every value is a confirmed REF6045 indicator, not a generic pattern. Rationale: Every domain/IP here is a confirmed REF6045 indicator (bancaporinternetbbmx[.]online is the phishing landing with a page-load Telegram notifier; 68.211.161.46 is the open-directory staging host) — direct IOC matches with essentially no benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/mexican-banking-fraud-scmbanker-ref6045 • https://gbhackers.com/ref6045-uses-scmbanker-powershell/ • https://cyberpress.org/clickfix-powers-mexican-fraud/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox hosts deliberately resolving the IOCs
  • Security researcher workstation browsing to the domains for analysis
  • Shared-IP hosting where 216.250.112.100/185.242.246.169 later host benign sites (re-validate ownership)
  • Proxy/DNS sinkhole logging the block itself
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process for the connection (browser vs powershell/cliente.ps1) and whether the destination is the phishing landing or a C2/staging IP. 2) Contain: block all listed domains and IPs at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate any host that resolved bancaporinternetbbmx[.]online or beaconed to the IPs. 3) Hunt: on hits, look for the full chain — Edge kiosk fakeupdate.net, bitsadmin from 68.211.161.46, run.vbs persistence, and clipboard CLABE swaps — and check for redirected credentials in the phishing panel timeframe.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("bancaporinternetbbmx.online","ratonvaquero2026.online","monteviral2026.duckdns.org","osogransd.online","negratomasa2026.online","gestionmontelavaria2026.online","ssinvestigaciones.com")
    or RemoteIP in ("68.211.161.46","216.250.112.100","185.242.246.169")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("bancaporinternetbbmx.online","ratonvaquero2026.online","monteviral2026.duckdns.org","osogransd.online","negratomasa2026.online","gestionmontelavaria2026.online","ssinvestigaciones.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| union (
    ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstIpAddr in ("68.211.161.46","216.250.112.100","185.242.246.169")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
  )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SCMBANKER Remote Utilities RAT host deployment (avs.ps1) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the SCMBANKER full-takeover stage where avs.ps1 silently installs the commercial Remote Utilities host for hands-on operator access. Article-specific because it ties the Remote Utilities host binaries (rutserv.exe/rfusclient.exe) to a PowerShell (avs.ps1) install path rather than legitimate IT deployment. Rationale: Elastic/GBHackers confirm avs.ps1 silently deploys a commercial Remote Utilities host for full takeover; tying rutserv.exe/rfusclient.exe (or the Remote Utilities file metadata) to an avs.ps1 PowerShell parent distinguishes malicious deployment from sanctioned IT use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/mexican-banking-fraud-scmbanker-ref6045 • https://gbhackers.com/ref6045-uses-scmbanker-powershell/
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organizations that legitimately license Remote Utilities for helpdesk (whitelist their signed deployment path/installer)
  • MSP remote-support sessions using Remote Utilities
  • Vendor support tooling bundling rfusclient.exe
  • Security team red-team RAT test
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "RemoteUtilities" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether Remote Utilities is a sanctioned tool in the org; if not, treat any execution as malicious. Check whether the install parent was avs.ps1 / run.vbs / powershell rather than an approved installer. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill rutserv.exe/rfusclient.exe, block the Remote Utilities relay/C2 IPs, and reset credentials used on the box. 3) Hunt: correlate to the SCMBANKER module chain (cliente.ps1 beacon, jujuzkt.ps1 banking monitor) and search the fleet for the same avs.ps1 install and Remote Utilities host installs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("rutserv.exe","rfusclient.exe")
    or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Remote Utilities"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Remote Utilities"
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "avs.ps1")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rutserv.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\rfusclient.exe"
    or (ParentProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "avs.ps1")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b30cb0aa977aacdab94d2ef503186c8f0b2fc10d7cf0d7c7c0ada70c127dc7e8", "554f1aefeb698995501751328c2f9fe93f02a680679fba3dd15f1ed93d46bf1b", "ff3555154e91e42490cc722b6c7f3c4c91654b7ef53a35d0719ffb89accf1b27") or SHA1 in~ ("b30cb0aa977aacdab94d2ef503186c8f0b2fc10d7cf0d7c7c0ada70c127dc7e8", "554f1aefeb698995501751328c2f9fe93f02a680679fba3dd15f1ed93d46bf1b", "ff3555154e91e42490cc722b6c7f3c4c91654b7ef53a35d0719ffb89accf1b27") or MD5 in~ ("b30cb0aa977aacdab94d2ef503186c8f0b2fc10d7cf0d7c7c0ada70c127dc7e8", "554f1aefeb698995501751328c2f9fe93f02a680679fba3dd15f1ed93d46bf1b", "ff3555154e91e42490cc722b6c7f3c4c91654b7ef53a35d0719ffb89accf1b27")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b30cb0aa977aacdab94d2ef503186c8f0b2fc10d7cf0d7c7c0ada70c127dc7e8", "554f1aefeb698995501751328c2f9fe93f02a680679fba3dd15f1ed93d46bf1b", "ff3555154e91e42490cc722b6c7f3c4c91654b7ef53a35d0719ffb89accf1b27") or SHA1 in~ ("b30cb0aa977aacdab94d2ef503186c8f0b2fc10d7cf0d7c7c0ada70c127dc7e8", "554f1aefeb698995501751328c2f9fe93f02a680679fba3dd15f1ed93d46bf1b", "ff3555154e91e42490cc722b6c7f3c4c91654b7ef53a35d0719ffb89accf1b27") or MD5 in~ ("b30cb0aa977aacdab94d2ef503186c8f0b2fc10d7cf0d7c7c0ada70c127dc7e8", "554f1aefeb698995501751328c2f9fe93f02a680679fba3dd15f1ed93d46bf1b", "ff3555154e91e42490cc722b6c7f3c4c91654b7ef53a35d0719ffb89accf1b27")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b30cb0aa977aacdab94d2ef503186c8f0b2fc10d7cf0d7c7c0ada70c127dc7e8", "554f1aefeb698995501751328c2f9fe93f02a680679fba3dd15f1ed93d46bf1b", "ff3555154e91e42490cc722b6c7f3c4c91654b7ef53a35d0719ffb89accf1b27"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GitHub 'Verified' Commits Can Be Rewritten Into New Hashes Without Breaking Signatures

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 6 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

New research shows that a signed Git commit's hash is not the one-of-a-kind name that much of the software world assumes it to be. Given any signed commit, someone without the signing key can mint a second commit with the same files, author, and date, and a valid signature, GitHub still stamps "Verified." Everything a reviewer would check matches. The commit's hash does not. That matters

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry

description: |

    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
