Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Better Auth: OAuth refresh-token replay via missing client authentication on oidc-provider and mcp plugins

Better Auth OAuth refresh_token grant replayed without client_secret (CVE-2026-53512) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts POST requests to the Better Auth legacy token endpoints (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token) that carry a refresh_token grant but present no client authentication (no Basic/Bearer Authorization header) and still receive a 200. Because these plugins never verify a confidential client's client_secret on the refresh path, a leaked refresh_token + public client_id lets an attacker mint tokens indefinitely via repeated rotation. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable endpoints (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token), the refresh path's missing Authorization header, and the rotation-replay behaviour (repeated 200s) described in CVE-2026-53512. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail left empty — this is self-hosted Node HTTP telemetry those platforms don't ship. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/better-auth/CVE-2026-53512/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5rr4-8452-hf4v
ATT&CKT1528 T1212
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PUBLIC clients (SPA/native + PKCE) correctly send no Authorization header on refresh — indistinguishable at the log layer without the oauthApplication client-type list
  • Aggressive mobile apps refreshing short-lived tokens every few minutes hit the >=3/hr threshold
  • Server-to-server integrations that place client_id/secret in the POST body rather than the Authorization header
  • Load-balancer or synthetic-monitoring probes that replay a stored refresh_token
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent) and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "HealthCheck" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "Datadog"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SrcIpAddr's full session and resolve the client_id being used; check the oauthApplication table — if that client's type is web/native/user-agent-based (confidential) it should NEVER refresh without client_secret, confirming abuse. 2) Contain: revoke the affected refresh chain — run db.deleteMany({model:"oauthAccessToken", where:[{field:"clientId", value: THAT_CLIENT_ID}]}) to invalidate all refresh tokens for the client, then rotate the client_secret. 3) Hunt: search for how the refresh_token leaked — XSS/log-capture/DB read; review the same SrcIp for prior /sso/register SSRF or access-token use at the victim user's scope.
let TokenEndpoints = dynamic(["/api/auth/oauth2/token","/api/auth/mcp/token"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has_any (TokenEndpoints)
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)   // no Basic/Bearer client auth on the refresh path
| where HttpStatusCode == 200                      // 200 == tokens minted successfully
| summarize Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Endpoints = make_set(Url) by SrcIpAddr, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| where Requests >= 3    // 3+ = rotation replay: attacker re-redeems the rotated refresh_token repeatedly
| order by Requests desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as Requests, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Web.url) as url, values(Web.status) as status from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method="POST" (Web.uri_path="/api/auth/oauth2/token" OR Web.uri_path="/api/auth/mcp/token") Web.status=200 by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent, Web.dest _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where Requests>=3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - Requests
| tstats summariesonly=false count as Requests, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Web.url) as url, values(Web.status) as status from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method="POST" (Web.uri_path="/api/auth/oauth2/token" OR Web.uri_path="/api/auth/mcp/token") Web.status=200 by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent, Web.dest _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where Requests>=3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - Requests
SSRF via Better Auth SSO provider registration to internal endpoints (CVE-2026-53513) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the server-side fetch primitive behind CVE-2026-53513: with skipDiscovery:true, POST /sso/register and /sso/update-provider persist attacker-supplied oidcConfig.userInfoEndpoint/tokenEndpoint/jwksEndpoint URLs, which better-auth then fetches server-side during the OIDC callback. Surfaces the auth tier making outbound OIDC-shaped HTTP requests to RFC1918/loopback/link-local addresses. Rationale: Grounded in the corroborated CVE-2026-53513 mechanism: skipDiscovery:true + attacker-controlled oidcConfig endpoints on /sso/register and /sso/update-provider drive server-side fetches; the high-fidelity pivot is the auth tier fetching OIDC paths against private IP space. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail empty — no web-egress equivalent for a self-hosted Node app in those feeds. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@better-auth/sso/CVE-2026-53513/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/sso
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately configured on-prem/internal IdP where the OIDC endpoints genuinely live on RFC1918 addresses (internal SSO)
  • Service-mesh/sidecar architectures where the app reaches an internal OIDC proxy at 127.0.0.1 or a cluster IP
  • Internal integration testing/staging registering a mock OIDC provider on a private host
  • Cloud metadata probes (169.254.169.254) from unrelated legitimate SDK calls sharing the proxy
Suppression filter
| where DstIpAddr != "127.0.0.1" and not (ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "169.254.169.254/32") and isempty(SrcHostname))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ssoProvider row(s) created/updated around the fetch and inspect oidcConfig.userInfoEndpoint/tokenEndpoint/jwksEndpoint — internal IPs, 127.0.0.1, or 169.254.169.254 confirm SSRF; note the authenticated session that called /sso/register. 2) Contain: delete/disable the malicious ssoProvider entries, block that session/user, and upgrade better-auth to >=1.6.11 (adds the public-routable host allowlist). 3) Hunt: review what the server-side fetch returned (reflected into user profile = non-blind SSRF) for cloud-metadata credentials or internal service data; check whether stolen metadata creds were then used against your cloud control plane.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr)
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) or ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "127.0.0.0/8") or ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "169.254.0.0/16")
| where Url has_any ("/.well-known/openid-configuration","userinfo","jwks","/token","oauth")   // OIDC fetch shapes reachable via a forged provider config
| summarize Fetches = count(), Paths = make_set(Url), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| order by Fetches desc
title: Better Auth SSO Provider Registration/Update Endpoint Accessed
id: 7b2e4c9a-3f61-4d28-9a5c-1e8f6b0d4c72
description: Flags POST requests to the Better Auth SSO provider registration endpoints abused by CVE-2026-53513 SSRF; analyst reviews the posted oidcConfig for internal/loopback URLs.
references:
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@better-auth/sso/CVE-2026-53513/
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5rr4-8452-hf4v

date: 2026/07/08

detection:
  selection:
    cs-method: POST

level: medium

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",dest) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",dest) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",dest) OR cidrmatch("127.0.0.0/8",dest) OR cidrmatch("169.254.0.0/16",dest)
| where match(url,"(?i)(openid-configuration|userinfo|/token|jwks|oauth)")

| where cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",dest) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",dest) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",dest) OR cidrmatch("127.0.0.0/8",dest) OR cidrmatch("169.254.0.0/16",dest)

Better Auth OIDC discovery probe followed by token/registration endpoint access (CVE-2026-53512/53513 recon) AIReconnaissance Low
Correlates a source that requests the OIDC discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration) and then, within 30 minutes, hits a sensitive Better Auth endpoint (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token, or /sso/register). Aims to catch pre-exploitation fingerprinting of grant types and endpoints preceding refresh-token replay or SSRF registration. Rationale: Chains the discovery-document probe to sensitive endpoint access from the same source within a tight window, reducing the enormous baseline noise of standalone /.well-known/openid-configuration requests. Explicitly low-confidence/hunting because the article body does not describe recon and the discovery doc is legitimately fetched by every SSO integration. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/better-auth/CVE-2026-53512/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/oidc-provider
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Every legitimate relying-party/SSO client fetches /.well-known/openid-configuration then calls /token as normal OAuth flow — this is the dominant FP
  • OIDC library cold-starts that refresh the discovery cache then immediately exchange tokens
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors polling discovery and token endpoints in sequence
  • Mobile SDKs that re-read discovery on app launch before refresh
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the SrcIp maps to a known registered relying party/client_id; a legitimate client will resolve cleanly, an unknown/external IP walking multiple endpoints will not. 2) Contain: if the source is unrecognised and followed the probe with a 200 on /token or a /sso/register POST, treat as UC1/UC2 and revoke the client's refresh chain / delete the ssoProvider row. 3) Hunt: pivot the SrcIp across UC1 (refresh replay) and UC2 (SSRF egress to private IPs) to confirm whether recon converted to exploitation.
let Window = 30m;
let Probes = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/.well-known/openid-configuration"
    | project ProbeTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, ProbeUrl = Url;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/api/auth/oauth2/token","/api/auth/mcp/token","/sso/register")
| join kind=inner Probes on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (ProbeTime .. ProbeTime + Window)
| project ProbeTime, AccessTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, ProbeUrl, TargetUrl = Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode
| order by AccessTime desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.uri_path="/.well-known/openid-configuration" OR Web.uri_path="/api/auth/oauth2/token" OR Web.uri_path="/api/auth/mcp/token" OR Web.uri_path="/sso/register") by Web.src, Web.uri_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| stats dc(uri_path) as distinct_paths, values(uri_path) as paths, min(firstTime) as firstTime, max(lastTime) as lastTime, sum(count) as total by src
| where distinct_paths>=2 AND mvcount(mvfilter(match(paths,"openid-configuration")))>0
| where (lastTime - firstTime) < 1800
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - total
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.uri_path="/.well-known/openid-configuration" OR Web.uri_path="/api/auth/oauth2/token" OR Web.uri_path="/api/auth/mcp/token" OR Web.uri_path="/sso/register") by Web.src, Web.uri_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Critical

RedWing MaaS Packages Android Bank Fraud as a Telegram Rental Service

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 11 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new Android malware operation called RedWing is being rented out on Telegram as a ready-made bank-fraud service. It lets even low-skill criminals take over a victim's phone, steal their banking logins, and capture the one-time codes that protect their accounts. Zimperium's zLabs, which found the operation, says it looks like a new variant of Oblivion, a $300-a-month rent-a-malware tool

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1486 T1555.003 T1566 T1566.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] RedWing dropper delivery: fake ProtonVPN APK and app-store-lookalike download hosts · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] RedWing Android banking trojan C2 beaconing to named panel domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
RedWing Android banking trojan C2 beaconing to named panel domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts corporate DNS/proxy/EDR-network telemetry for resolution of or connection to RedWing MaaS command-and-control panel hosts (redwing.top, redwingqq.top, krusty-crabs.sbs, and the Cloudflare Workers relay api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev). Any managed or BYOD device — including Android endpoints enrolled in MDE — touching these hosts indicates a live RedWing infection phoning home to receive overlay targets, stream the screen, or exfiltrate SMS/OTP data. Rationale: Uses the four RedWing C2/panel hosts (redwing.top, redwingqq.top, krusty-crabs.sbs, api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev) from Zimperium's zLabs IOC bundle — corroborated against the primary vendor blog, distinct from the THN article text. Named C2 domains are the highest-fidelity anchor available since the kit is reskinned and app-name tracking is unreliable. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/redwing-a-mobile-malware-as-a-service-operation • https://github.com/Zimperium/IOC/tree/master/2026-07-RedWing
ATT&CKT1437.001 T1481
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst detonating a RedWing sample in a corporate malware sandbox that egresses through the same DNS/proxy
  • Automated TI enrichment connector (Anomali/Recorded Future/urlscan) resolving the domains for verification
  • Safe Links / proxy URL-rewrite prefetch resolving a submitted link without user intent
  • DNS sinkhole already redirecting the domain — query is logged but connection is benign
  • Security awareness / red-team exercise seeding the domain internally
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the client device/IP that resolved the C2 host and confirm it is a real user endpoint (especially an enrolled Android/BYOD device) rather than a sandbox or TI scanner; check for repeated/beaconing hits vs a one-off lookup. 2) CONTAIN: Block the four domains at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate or quarantine the offending device via MDM/EDR, and force a corporate credential + banking-app password reset for the user; check for attacker-set call forwarding (*21*) on the carrier account. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the resolved IPs and on the distribution domains (manyrei.live, wmanyrei.icu, yandex-disk.net, offservers.ru) across the estate, and review the device for a recently sideloaded APK with hidden icon and Accessibility grants.
let C2Hosts = dynamic(["redwing.top","redwingqq.top","krusty-crabs.sbs","api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (C2Hosts)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Hosts = dynamic(["redwing.top","redwingqq.top","krusty-crabs.sbs","api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev"]);
union
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has_any (C2Hosts)
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="DNS", Device=Computer, Client=ClientIP, Indicator=Name),
(CommonSecurityLog
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DestinationHostName has_any (C2Hosts) or RequestURL has_any (C2Hosts)
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="Proxy/FW", Device=SourceHostName, Client=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RedWing dropper delivery: fake ProtonVPN APK and app-store-lookalike download hosts AIDelivery High
Hunts web/proxy/DNS/EDR-network telemetry for contact with the RedWing distribution infrastructure that serves the sideloaded dropper — the fake Proton_VPN.apk on manyrei.live plus the lookalike/typosquat delivery hosts wmanyrei.icu, yandex-disk.net (impersonating Yandex Disk) and offservers.ru. A corporate or managed device fetching an .apk from these hosts marks the initial-access sideload stage before Accessibility abuse and overlay injection begin. Rationale: Anchored on the RedWing distribution URLs from Zimperium's zLabs IOC bundle — manyrei.live/Proton_VPN.apk (the masqueraded ProtonVPN dropper) plus wmanyrei.icu, the Yandex-Disk typosquat yandex-disk.net, and offservers.ru — corroborated by the vendor blog. The literal 'Proton_VPN.apk' filename and the specific hosts are article-specific delivery-stage indicators, and an .apk fetch on a corporate egress is inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/redwing-a-mobile-malware-as-a-service-operation • https://github.com/Zimperium/IOC/tree/master/2026-07-RedWing
ATT&CKT1660 T1655
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User genuinely searching for Yandex Disk and mistyping to the yandex-disk.net typosquat (visit is still suspicious but not the trojan)
  • Malware analyst/red team downloading the sample for testing through corporate egress
  • URL sandbox/detonation service (proxy DLP, Safe Links) fetching the .apk to scan it
  • Threat-intel connector resolving the distribution domains for enrichment
  • Proxy content-inspection prefetch touching the host without a real user click
Suppression filter
// Sentinel: drop known detonation/scanner egress and require a real client
| where Client !in ("<proxy_sandbox_ip>") // remove line or keep as-is if no sandbox egress IP; alternatively exclude by device
| where Device !has "sandbox" and Device !has "malware-lab"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether the request actually retrieved an .apk (check HTTP method/response size and user-agent) and whether the client is a user endpoint versus a scanner; identify the referring phishing/fake-store URL from proxy logs. 2) CONTAIN: Block the distribution domains and the Proton_VPN.apk path at proxy/DNS/firewall, and if an Android device fetched it, isolate via MDM and block sideloading + the default-SMS/Accessibility roles for the app. 3) HUNT: Pivot the client to the C2 detection (redwing.top / redwingqq.top / krusty-crabs.sbs / api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev) to confirm post-install beaconing, and sweep EmailUrlInfo/proxy for other recipients of the same lure link.
let DropHosts = dynamic(["manyrei.live","wmanyrei.icu","yandex-disk.net","offservers.ru"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (DropHosts) or RemoteUrl has "Proton_VPN.apk"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let DropHosts = dynamic(["manyrei.live","wmanyrei.icu","yandex-disk.net","offservers.ru"]);
union
(CommonSecurityLog
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DestinationHostName has_any (DropHosts) or RequestURL has_any (DropHosts) or RequestURL has "Proton_VPN.apk"
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="Proxy/FW", Device=SourceHostName, Client=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationHostName)),
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has_any (DropHosts)
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="DNS", Device=Computer, Client=ClientIP, Indicator=Name)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time

         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue Agent Flaw Could Have Let Attackers Hijack Google Dialogflow CX Chatbots

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 13 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A critical flaw in Google's Dialogflow CX could have let an attacker with edit rights on one Code Block-enabled agent compromise other Code Block-enabled agents in the same Google Cloud project. From there, they could read live conversations, steal the data users shared, and make the bots send attacker-written messages, including requests to re-enter a password. Security firm Varonis found it

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] IAM grant of Dialogflow edit rights (dialogflow.playbooks.update) — Rogue Agent pre-condition
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Dialogflow CX runtime exceptions revealing malicious Code Block execution · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Rogue Agent Flaw Could Have Let Attackers Hijack Google Dialogflow CX Chatbots
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Dialogflow CX Code Block hijack: UpdatePlaybook DATA_WRITE from anomalous developer identity · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Dialogflow CX Code Block hijack: UpdatePlaybook DATA_WRITE from anomalous developer identity AIInstallation High
Hunts the Varonis 'Rogue Agent' entry point — the dialogflow.playbooks.update permission being exercised via the UpdatePlaybook API, which is the ONLY customer-visible trace of an attacker injecting a malicious Code Block. Surfaces every playbook update with the calling principal, source IP and project so analysts can spot updates from compromised dev accounts or insiders acting off-hours / from new IPs. Rationale: Uses the exact GCP audit methodName google.cloud.dialogflow.cx.v3(beta1).Playbooks.UpdatePlaybook mapped to the dialogflow.playbooks.update permission (DATA_WRITE) named in the article as the whole entry point; method name confirmed against Google Cloud Dialogflow CX audit-logging docs. Sentinel/Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty — this telemetry is GCP audit logs with no equivalent in those platforms' canonical schemas. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gcp-dialogflow-vulnerability/ • https://docs.cloud.google.com/dialogflow/cx/docs/concept/audit-logging
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1648
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chatbot developers legitimately editing Playbooks or Code Blocks during business hours
  • CI/CD service accounts pushing agent updates via Terraform / gcloud
  • Bulk playbook migrations across environments (dev→prod promotion)
  • Vendor / consultant accounts with temporary edit rights doing approved changes
Suppression filter
| search NOT "data.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail"="*gserviceaccount.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the principalEmail + callerIp for the UpdatePlaybook event; confirm the identity is a known Dialogflow developer and the IP/time matches their baseline. Diff the updated Code Block against the approved version in the console (attacker may have restored the console copy while the runtime file stays overwritten). 2) Contain: if the principal or IP is unrecognized, revoke dialogflow.playbooks.update / the Dialogflow editor role from that account, rotate its credentials, and force-redeploy affected agents to reset the shared Cloud Run container. 3) Hunt: enumerate every account/role holding dialogflow.playbooks.update project-wide, review all UpdatePlaybook events from the same principal/IP, and check Dialogflow runtime error logs for Code Block exceptions.
title: Dialogflow CX Playbook Update (Rogue Agent Code Block Injection Entry Point)
id: 8f3d2c1a-6b4e-4f9a-9c2d-1a7e5b0c9d34
description: Detects UpdatePlaybook Data Access audit events in Dialogflow CX, the sole customer-visible trace of the Varonis Rogue Agent Code Block hijack (dialogflow.playbooks.update).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/rogue-agent-flaw-could-have-let.html
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/gcp-dialogflow-vulnerability/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.t1078.004
  - attack.t1648
logsource:
  product: gcp
  service: gcp.audit

  selection:
    gcp.audit.method_name:
      - google.cloud.dialogflow.cx.v3beta1.Playbooks.UpdatePlaybook
      - google.cloud.dialogflow.cx.v3.Playbooks.UpdatePlaybook
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate chatbot developers editing playbooks / Code Blocks
level: medium
source:gcp.audit @protoPayload.methodName:(google.cloud.dialogflow.cx.v3beta1.Playbooks.UpdatePlaybook OR google.cloud.dialogflow.cx.v3.Playbooks.UpdatePlaybook)
CLOUD
sourcetype="google:gcp:pubsub:message" ("data.protoPayload.methodName"="google.cloud.dialogflow.cx.v3beta1.Playbooks.UpdatePlaybook" OR "data.protoPayload.methodName"="google.cloud.dialogflow.cx.v3.Playbooks.UpdatePlaybook")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values("data.protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp") as src_ip values("data.protoPayload.resourceName") as playbook by "data.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail" "data.resource.labels.project_id"

Dialogflow CX runtime exceptions revealing malicious Code Block execution AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the second article-recommended check: failed Dialogflow requests whose error messages leak Python exceptions thrown by an injected/overwritten Code Block (e.g. urllib egress to an attacker server, or a botched code_execution_env.py overwrite). Surfaces ERROR-severity Dialogflow API events so analysts can read the exception text a malicious block produces. Rationale: Directly implements the article's 'run a Cloud Logging query for failed user requests, where the error messages can reveal exceptions thrown by malicious Code Blocks' guidance, scoped to serviceName dialogflow.googleapis.com and ERROR/non-zero status. GCP-only telemetry, so non-GCP query fields are intentionally empty; Sigma skipped because triage depends on reading free-text exception messages rather than a single fixed field match. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gcp-dialogflow-vulnerability/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/rogue-agent-flaw-could-have-let.html
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1648
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine bugs in developer-written Code Blocks throwing Python exceptions
  • Malformed end-user input causing input-validation code to raise
  • Dialogflow webhook/tool timeouts unrelated to Code Blocks
  • Transient GCP service errors (503/quota) returned to the caller
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the error_messages / status.message text for Python tracebacks referencing urllib, requests, socket, open('code_execution_env.py'), or unexpected external hostnames. Correlate the affected project/agent with any recent UpdatePlaybook event. 2) Contain: if a traceback shows outbound network or file-overwrite behaviour, disable the offending agent's Code Blocks, redeploy to reset the shared container, and open a case with Google Cloud support (the overwrite lives in Google-managed infra). 3) Hunt: pull all UpdatePlaybook events for that project, review who holds dialogflow.playbooks.update, and search for repeated identical exceptions indicating a persistent injected block.
source:gcp.audit @protoPayload.serviceName:dialogflow.googleapis.com @severity:ERROR
CLOUD
sourcetype="google:gcp:pubsub:message" "data.protoPayload.serviceName"="dialogflow.googleapis.com" ("data.severity"="ERROR" OR "data.protoPayload.status.code">0)
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values("data.protoPayload.methodName") as methods values("data.protoPayload.status.message") as error_messages values("data.protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp") as src_ip by "data.resource.labels.project_id" "data.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail"
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
IAM grant of Dialogflow edit rights (dialogflow.playbooks.update) — Rogue Agent pre-condition AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts new IAM bindings that hand an identity a role carrying dialogflow.playbooks.update (roles/dialogflow.admin, roles/dialogflow.consoleAgentEditor / API editor), the single permission that turns a content-edit right into arbitrary Python execution in the shared Code Block runtime. Flags who granted it, to whom, and in which project. Rationale: Targets the article's 'audit which roles and accounts hold dialogflow.playbooks.update' guidance by detecting the moment such a role is granted via SetIamPolicy policyDelta bindingDeltas (standard GCP IAM audit structure). Dialogflow-specific roles keep FP low; GCP-only telemetry so non-GCP fields are empty and Sigma is skipped (policyDelta binding-role match is awkward as a single-field selection across GCP Sigma taxonomies). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/rogue-agent-flaw-could-have-let.html • https://docs.cloud.google.com/dialogflow/cx/docs/concept/audit-logging
ATT&CKT1098.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Onboarding a new chatbot developer to a Dialogflow project
  • IaC (Terraform) applying a project's baseline IAM policy
  • Org admin granting a support vendor temporary Dialogflow access
  • Group-based role assignment during a team reorg
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the granting principal is authorized to change IAM and that the grantee is a legitimate Dialogflow developer; check whether the grant coincided with an out-of-hours or new-IP session. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, remove the binding, disable/rotate the grantee and grantor credentials, and review any UpdatePlaybook events made by the grantee since the grant. 3) Hunt: enumerate all current holders of dialogflow.playbooks.update across every project, alert on any that are service accounts or external identities, and baseline expected Dialogflow editors so future grants stand out.
source:gcp.audit @protoPayload.methodName:SetIamPolicy @protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas.action:ADD @protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas.role:(roles/dialogflow.admin OR roles/dialogflow.consoleAgentEditor OR roles/dialogflow.agentEditor OR roles/dialogflow.apiAdmin)
CLOUD
sourcetype="google:gcp:pubsub:message" "data.protoPayload.methodName"="SetIamPolicy" "data.protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas.action"="ADD" "data.protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas.role"="roles/dialogflow.*"
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime by "data.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail" "data.protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas.member" "data.protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas.role" "data.resource.labels.project_id" "data.protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp"
| convert ctime(firstTime)
| sort - firstTime
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName

                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceFileEvents

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc
